title: MB0-03101
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXX, the claimant, 34 years of age, the claimant, is claiming under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

In her Personal Information Form (PIF), filed with the tribunal on July 12, 2010, the claimant alleges that in her country, she was the victim of the authority and violence of her brothers. She alleges that she had been earning a living by working in XXXXX since 2000. At the beginning of 2006, one of her brothers, XXXX, forced her to marry a wealthy Saudi Arabian man. The marriage took place on XXXXX, 2006. No documents were signed because, according to the claimant, this Saudi man had to obtain an authorization in his country in order for their marriage to be official. After a honeymoon in Tunisia, the claimant returned to Algeria and he returned to Saudi Arabia. Between the end of 2006 and the summer of 2007, the claimant alleges that she saw this Saudi man several times. In XXXX 2007, she met him in Egypt. That is when he was allegedly violent toward her. In XXXXX 2007, she returned to Algeria, and he supposedly exercised [translation] "control from afar" over her. Between the end of 2007 and the year 2008, this Saudi man visited her every other month for a short time. At the end of XXXXX 2008, she found out that she was pregnant, and because of that, wanted to make their marriage official. Her supposed husband allegedly demanded that she have an abortion and hit her. In XXXXX 2009, she had a miscarriage. In XXXXX 2009, she found out that this Saudi man was married to another woman. She tried desperately to persuade him to marry her, going to Lebanon in XXXXX 2009. In XXXXX 2009, she applied for a Canadian visa, which she obtained with the help of a Canadian friend. In XXXXX 2009, she had an operation related to her miscarriage. She then met her supposed husband in Spain to ask him for money for her trip to Canada. She then left her country on XXXXX, 2010, and claimed refugee protection on XXXXX, 2010.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee." The claimant is also not a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.

The claimant's identity has been established to the panel's satisfaction, based on a copy of her passport issued by the Algerian authorities, which Immigration filed as evidence. The panel concludes that it is an acceptable identity document under section 106 of the IRPA.

In assessing the testimony before it, the panel took into account the Chairperson's Guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution1 before rendering its decision. The claimant was not credible, and her testimony was not trustworthy with respect to the essential elements of her claim for refugee protection.

Basically, the claimant testified that she feared returning to Algeria by reason of her membership in a particular social group-women-and because she allegedly suffered violence at the hands of her brothers and a Saudi man named XXXXXXXXXXX.

The claimant is a woman who expresses herself very well in French, who describes herself as active and who had been working in XXXXX since 2000. She was a XXXXXXXXXXX. She performed XXXXXXXXX tasks [translation] "in the office" and XXXXXXXXX tasks "outside the office," such as XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. That is supposedly XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She also alleges in her PIF that she is an open, modern person, unlike her very conservative brothers.2

First of all, the panel noted a major contradiction between the claimant's testimony and her PIF when she was asked on what date she supposedly married this Saudi man. She testified that it was XXXXX, 2006, and that she would never forget that date.

According to question 3 of her PIF, however, she was married on XXXXX, 2006. She was therefore asked whether there was a reason for such a discrepancy. She repeated that she was indeed married on XXXXX, 2006. Once again, the panel asked her whether there was a reason that would explain this discrepancy. She then stated, [translation] "It's a mistake" and stated that she was married on XXXXX, 2006.

The panel rejects this explanation by the claimant as inadequate. First of all, it is implausible in the circumstances described, considering that it was allegedly a date that she would never forget, that the claimant could have made such a mistake. This marriage is at the very heart of her claim. The panel is of the opinion that it can draw a negative conclusion from this as to the claimant's credibility.

Furthermore, the claimant testified that she lived with her family until the end of 2008, despite her marriage, which supposedly took place in 2006, and that she then went to live in the apartment XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She supposedly still continued to go back and forth between the family home, where she still lived sometimes, and this apartment, where she supposedly lived alone with her mother.

Neither at question 31 of her PIF nor at question 11 of her PIF does it state that she went back and forth between these two residences. Asked why she did not mention this before the day of her hearing, she stated that she had not known she had to, that she had made a mistake, that she had not thought of it, and finally, [translation] "I should have put both."

The panel is not satisfied with these explanations. It found out on the day of the hearing that she supposedly lived between the home of this Saudi man and the family home until she left Algeria. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's credibility is undermined in relation to this purported marriage.

In addition, the claimant testified that, since 2006, she had been a victim of violence by her brothers, as well as by this Saudi man. She waited four years before leaving Algeria, for reasons that will be detailed below. She stated that she came to Canada in 2010 for a break and that she had not planned to claim refugee protection, since she did not even know that she could do so. Supposedly, it was only much later-about a month after her arrival in the country-that she found this out.

However, at question 24(b) of her PIF, the claimant clearly states that she claimed refugee protection three days after she arrived in the country-on XXXXX, 2010. Asked to explain this discrepancy between her testimony and her PIF, the claimant once again replied, [translation] "I must have made a mistake."

The panel is not satisfied with the claimant's explanation whereby she stated that she had made a mistake every time her testimony diverged. Claiming refugee protection three days after her arrival and testifying that she did so long after her arrival because she did not even know that refugee protection existed in Canada are very different things. The panel therefore draws a negative inference as to the claimant's credibility in relation to her fear.
But what is even more important in terms of the credibility of this story is the implausibility raised by the claimant's testimony and her narrative.

The claimant testified that she lived in a very conservative family, under the thumb of her family, her brothers and then of this Saudi man, and in spite of all that, managed to work in the XXXXX business for 10 years, even acting as a XXXXXXXXXXXX the office to XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX. Her passport3 also clearly shows that she was able to travel outside her country. Before her marriage, she appears to have gone to Malaysia and even to France.

Asked to explain how she could have done all that if her family and this Saudi man had so much control over her, she claimed that she was working to earn money for her brothers, who were using drugs, and that she was able to leave her country before her marriage because she travelled with her sister, who was married.

But on top of that, throughout her testimony, the claimant alleged that what she wanted most of all-despite never having wanted this religious marriage-was to make this marriage official so that she could then get divorced and eventually remarry.

So, all these years when she supposedly endured the violence of her brothers and this Saudi man, she had only this solution, according to her testimony: make the union official, even going as far as using her alleged pregnancy by this Saudi man to force him to make this marriage official, so that she could get divorced and eventually remarry.

In the panel's opinion, it is implausible that a woman with a profile such as that of the claimant, who travelled for her work (see in particular para. 18) and who claims to have suffered from these experiences, would give more priority to her desire to get married to facilitate a divorce, than to her fear for her life.

The panel asked her why she waited so long to leave her country, given that she claimed to be a victim of her brothers and of this Saudi man and also that, at any point, she would have had occasion to be alone, either at work or at this apartment with her mother, and why she did not do what she needed to do to save herself before that. She responded that she could not do it because she always obtained these exit visas through this Saudi man-to whom she referred during the hearing sometimes as [translation] "my partner" and sometimes as "my husband," explaining during the hearing that she was "his wife" or that she was not "the wife" of this Saudi man-and she repeated that her only solution was to get married to facilitate a divorce and eventually remarry.

However, it was through a female Canadian friend that she obtained her visa to leave and come to Canada in 2010.4 Question 31 of her PIF even indicates that she hid this exit visa from this Saudi man. She also added that this trip was not planned-[translation] "It just came up," I just came here to rest.

The panel rejects these explanations as unsatisfactory to justify such a delay in leaving her country when she claims to have been a victim of this violence during all that time. Although the panel recognizes that the documentary evidence indicates that Algerian women may be subject to the authoritarianism of their families, particularly male family members, it is of the opinion that the claimant does not fit this profile, based on what she herself alleged about herself:5 she worked, had an income, went out alone without being subject to her brothers and even less so to this Saudi man who spent most of his time in Saudi Arabia, as she herself testified.

In addition, the panel draws a negative inference from the fact that the claimant constantly changed how she referred to this Saudi man. This further undermines her credibility with regard to her story of a forced marriage.

The panel reiterates that, in its opinion, the need to flee to save herself and the fear for her life should have had priority over the desire to marry to facilitate a divorce and ultimately remarry. It draws a negative inference from this, which undermines the claimant's credibility with regard to this story of a forced marriage and her fear of returning.
The panel rejects the claimant's testimony as not credible. It therefore attaches no probative value to exhibits P-1 and P-2.6

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant has failed to discharge her burden of establishing the existence of a serious possibility that she would be persecuted on one of the Convention grounds or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to her life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she were to return to her country.
For these reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim of XXXXXXXXXXX.
